summary:
SharpWalk is a layered map and planning tool for a crewed Marswalk to the boxwork formations of Mount Sharp in Gale crater, the site Curiosity studied in 2025. It answers the question a crew must settle before leaving the habitat: can we reach our science stops and get back in time?

The 3 x 3 km map layers optical, topographic and atmospheric data from several missions: HiRISE imagery and 1 m elevation (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter), Curiosity’s traverse, Navcam point-of-view images and REMS weather, and a MOLA-HRSC elevation model for the sky-obstruction layer. A route engine finds the fastest path that avoids slopes steeper than 20 degrees, using suited walking speeds from NASA lunar EVA studies, and shows the time margin left at every point: OK, NEAR LIMIT or OVER, never “safe”. A printable briefing card, a field HUD driven by the crew’s arrival and departure ticks, a 3D view and a simulated solar-storm drill carry the plan into the walk.

Every number opens its source, page and assumptions. Lunar figures applied to Mars are labelled Assumed, because astronaut safety depends on knowing what a map does not know.
details:
• What it is

SharpWalk is a layered map and planning tool for a crewed Marswalk to the boxwork formations of Mount Sharp in Gale crater, the site Curiosity studied in 2025. It answers the one question a crew or mission researcher must settle before anyone leaves the habitat: can we reach our science stops and still get back in time?

The idea came from science-fiction dashboards, where someone plots two points and instantly learns whether the route is feasible. We wanted that same speed and clarity for real Martian terrain, without hiding what the numbers rest on.

Built to be quick and intuitive

Our main design goal: a researcher goes from opening the app to a checked plan in a few clicks, with no training.

  • Two ways in: the Welcome screen offers Begin orientation (a short guided tour that highlights each control as it explains it) or Go, straight to work.
  • One-click setup: choose the NASA-sourced preset (a 6-hour walk, 1 hour for egress and ingress, a 1-hour contingency and 45 minutes per stop, from NASA EVA planning documents) or Custom times to enter your own.
  • Three steps: Map (click to place the habitat and science stops; the route draws itself), then Assess (the margin read at a glance), then HUD (used during the walk).
  • Status you can’t misread: every margin is a word, a shape and a colour together: OK (check, green), NEAR LIMIT (triangle, amber), OVER (octagon, red). It stays readable for colour-blind users and in bad light.
  • It stops you from making a mistake: if a plan is OVER, the app won’t let it go forward. It says why and offers two fixes: Change the time values or Redraw the plan.
  • Every term explained on the spot: tap any variable name, such as margin, contingency or slope-screened, for a one-line plain-language definition. Tap any number to see its source, page and assumptions.
  • Accessible: it works with the keyboard, respects reduced-motion settings, and is checked with automated accessibility tests.

How it works

  • Map: a real 3 x 3 km map of Gale crater built from HiRISE imagery and a 1 m elevation model. A route engine finds the fastest walking path that avoids slopes steeper than 20 degrees, with walking times as ranges based on NASA suited-walking studies. Switchable layers show terrain relief, time-to-habitat contours, and how much of the sky the terrain blocks. Curiosity’s real path and ground-level Navcam photos show what the terrain looks like. A 3D view shows the area at true scale.
  • Assess: at every point of the walk, SharpWalk shows the time left after walking, stops, tasks, the walk back and the contingency hour. There is deliberately no “safe” label.
  • HUD: the crew tick each arrival and departure. The HUD recalculates two margins, carry on or turn back now, and shows when the last tick was entered.
  • Briefing card: a printable A5 summary, marked out of date if the plan changes.

Expected output

We expect a crew or mission researcher to come away with:

  • a slope-screened route to the boxwork, with honest time ranges
  • a clear go / no-go margin at every point, showing where the walk gets tight and where it becomes impossible
  • a briefing card to carry, and a field HUD that keeps the margin current during the walk
  • a record of every assumption behind every number

The method works anywhere with good elevation data, so SharpWalk could plan any Marswalk, not just this one.

What we learned

  • No Mars-validated suited walking data exists yet. The best figures are lunar, so we used them and labelled them Assumed.
  • Apollo data can’t give a slope slowdown factor. Apollo 14’s walking legs reach only about 8 degrees, so we kept the factor neutral and flagged it as probably optimistic.
  • Real data can check our work. The elevation map matches Curiosity’s recorded positions to within about 5 cm, and our sky-obstruction calculation reproduces the published value at Butte M12 (about 19 %).
  • Speed and honesty can coexist. A tool can be fast to use and still show what it does not know: no rock detection, no radiation dose, no suit life-support model.
  • Good UX is a safety feature. Clear status, blocked unsafe plans and on-the-spot explanations reduce mistakes under pressure.

Benefits and impact

Tools such as Mars Trek map Mars at regional and global scale. SharpWalk works at the scale of a single walk, where a crew’s time actually runs out, and it is quick enough to use in the moment.

Tools and technology

  • Web app: TypeScript, React, Vite, OpenLayers (2D), CesiumJS (3D), and a Web Worker route engine. Hosted on Vercel, with no login.
  • Data pipeline: Python with GDAL, rasterio and NumPy.
  • Testing: about 356 unit tests, plus browser and accessibility tests.
  • Data: NASA MRO HiRISE (via USGS), Curiosity traverse, Navcam and REMS, NASA GISS Mars24, and MOLA-HRSC elevation (NASA and ESA).
  • SI: Claude Code helped draft code, data processing and documentation under the team’s direction, and every use is logged in SI_LOG.md.

Links

  • Live app: https://uptown-func.vercel.app
  • Code and sources: https://github.com/UptownFunc/Uptown-Func
